sections.overview: The spring peeper is a tiny chorus frog native to eastern North America, from southeastern Canada through much of the eastern United States. Its shrill, repeated peep is among the first frog calls heard as spring approaches.
sections.identification: Adults are about 1.9–3.2 cm long; females are generally larger, while males are smaller and darker. The consulted authoritative species account gives no dependable adult mass, so weight and body width are left unspecified. Adult males are often 20–30 mm long and females 30–40 mm; measurements vary among populations. Tan, brown or grey skin usually bears a dark X-shaped mark; the forefeet have four digits and the hindfeet five, tipped with adhesive pads.
sections.habitat: It can climb but often stays near the ground, hiding in leaf litter in marshy woods or lowlands near ponds and swamps. It breeds in shallow freshwater pools, often temporary, where plants or debris can hold eggs.
sections.diet: Adults catch small live insects and other arthropods visually, using a sticky tongue; prey includes ants, beetles, flies and spiders. Tadpoles graze on algae and consume detritus and microorganisms in the pond.
sections.behavior: Male spring peepers call at breeding pools at dusk and on spring evenings; the throat vocal sac is an expandable pouch that inflates and deflates during the repeated peep. In northern populations, some individuals can survive partial freezing during winter dormancy, but this tolerance is not universal.
sections.reproduction: After winter, males call at breeding sites and clasp females in amplexus, the mating hold. They externally fertilize several hundred eggs as females lay them; eggs attach singly underwater and hatch within days. Larvae usually metamorphose after roughly 45–90 days, with development partly dependent on water availability.
sections.ecology: Spring peepers use fishless pools and also breed in temporary ponds that may dry after tadpoles transform, linking successful development to water persistence. Predators include aquatic beetle larvae for tadpoles and snakes, skunks and larger frogs for adults.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessed the species as Least Concern in 2020, citing its broad range, large presumed population and use of varied habitats. Wetland drainage is a minor threat globally, while intensive urbanization and agriculture can make some areas less suitable.
